meta.descriptionEn: On 18 October 1967 a small Soviet capsule fell into the clouds of Venus. For 93 minutes it descended, parachuting through the atmosphere and measuring a world no probe had ever analysed from the inside. What it found shocked scientists: a crushing atmosphere of carbon dioxide, a surprisingly weak magnetic field and almost no water. Yet the story did not end cleanly. Mission teams first announced that the probe had reached the surface, then a radar puzzle and a flyby from an American spacecraft revealed the truth. Discover how Venera 4 was built, how it survived entry, what it sent home, and how a misread signal changed the way we understand our hellish sister planet.
meta.descriptionUr: 18 October 1967 ko ek chhota Soviet capsule Venus ke badlon mein gir gaya. 93 minute tak woh parachute ke saath utarta raha aur aisi duniya ko andar se naapta raha jahan pehle koi probe tajziya nahi kar saka tha. Jo data aya usne scientists ko hairan kar diya: bhaari carbon dioxide wali fizaa, kamzor magnetic field aur na-ke-barabar pani. Lekin kahani itni seedhi nahi thi. Pehle ailaan hua ke probe sathh tak pahunch gaya, phir radar ki ghalat fehmi aur Mariner 5 ke data ne sach saamne rakha. Dekhiye Venera 4 ki poori kahani.

articleEn: On 18 October 1967, a small Soviet capsule called Venera 4 was plunging toward the clouds of Venus. As it entered the atmosphere, its heat shield reached 11,000 °C and the capsule began to slow rapidly. At one moment the deceleration inside hit 300 G, or three hundred times the pull of Earth's gravity.

Then, at an altitude of about 52 kilometres, the parachute opened. A historic moment began: for the first time, data was flowing back to Earth from inside another planet's atmosphere. Venera 4 was the first spacecraft to enter the atmosphere of another planet and survive. But the question was what would happen next.

This article tells the full story of that journey, built around three big questions. First: what kind of place is Venus? What is the temperature beneath the clouds, how heavy is the air, and which gases does it contain? Second: did the probe actually reach the planet's surface? The Soviet team's first answer was yes, but was it correct?
The third question is why that first claim turned out to be wrong. Behind it lay a small technical misunderstanding, one that turned the whole conclusion upside down.

articleEn: Venus is often called Earth's sister or twin. Its diameter is 12,103.6 kilometres, only 638.4 kilometres less than Earth's, and its mass is 81.5 percent of Earth's. Given such similarities, some people thought conditions there might resemble those on Earth.

The problem was that thick clouds cover Venus completely. Through a telescope, no surface features can be seen. In the 1920s, ultraviolet images revealed some detail, but even that did not show what lay under the clouds. Even the planet's rotation was a mystery. Work in the 1950s later showed that it spins in the opposite direction.

Where science is silent, stories speak. From the 1930s to the 1950s, science fiction often portrayed Venus as hot but habitable. Scientists, however, lacked real numbers. Estimates of surface pressure ranged from a few atmospheres to hundreds. Imagine having to build a capsule that might operate in a few atmospheres, or in hundreds. How strong would you make it? This was the dilemma facing Soviet engineers, and the early flights were not easy.

The first attempt came on 4 February 1961, and that probe could not leave Earth orbit. It was announced as Tyazhely Sputnik, or Heavy Satellite, because failed missions were not announced at the time. Venera 1 launched on 12 February 1961, but seven days later its telemetry failed and contact was lost. By one estimate it passed about 100,000 kilometres from Venus and still orbits the Sun today.

Venera 2 launched on 12 November 1965 and met a similar fate: after leaving Earth orbit, its telemetry failed. Then came Venera 3. On 1 March 1966 it struck the surface of Venus, so the first human-made object reached another planet. But its scientific instruments failed as it entered the atmosphere, so not a single measurement came back. A great opportunity ended without data.

Meanwhile, the United States' Mariner 2 flew past Venus on 14 December 1962, completing the first successful interplanetary mission. It passed 34,833 kilometres from the planet and collected atmospheric data. But a flyby could not look inside the atmosphere, and no probe had yet sent measurements from within the clouds back to Earth.
The question was simple: how hot and how heavy is the air there? The Venera 4 team had to answer it, and for that they needed a capsule that could survive unknown conditions.

articleEn: Venera 4 was actually the name for two parts: a carrier spacecraft and a landing capsule. The carrier stood 3.5 metres tall, with solar panels 4 metres across and an area of 2.5 square metres. It carried a 2-metre magnetometer, an ion detector, a cosmic ray detector, and an ultraviolet spectrometer that could detect hydrogen and oxygen gases.

At the rear was a liquid-fuel thruster for course corrections along the way, and 127 different commands could be sent from Earth. The plan was that on reaching Venus, the carrier would release the capsule and break apart.

The real story was the capsule. It was roughly spherical, 1 metre in diameter and weighing 383 kilograms. The heat shield carried the main burden. It was improved over earlier Venera probes and could withstand up to 11,000 °C. The cooling system changed too: instead of a liquid-based design, a simpler and more reliable gas system was used.

Then came testing. The capsule was tried in three separate installations, facing higher temperatures, pressure and rapidly increasing speed. A high-temperature vacuum system recreated upper-atmosphere conditions to check its heat resistance. Pressure of up to 25 atmospheres was then applied, though nobody knew the real surface pressure of Venus. Finally, a centrifuge subjected it to acceleration of up to 450 g. In that test, cracks appeared in electronic components and cable brackets. Those parts were replaced shortly before launch. Time was short, because missing the launch window would mean losing the right days for the journey.

The designers also considered what would happen if the capsule landed on water. It could float, and its lock was made of sugar. On contact with water the sugar would dissolve and free the transmitter antennas. It also had a new vibration-damping system, and its parachute could withstand up to 450 °C.

Inside were an altimeter, thermal control, thermometer, barometer, hydrometer and gas analysis instruments: in effect a small scientific laboratory. Two transmitters working at 922 MHz sent data at just 1 bit per second, with a new measurement every 48 seconds. They were to switch on as the parachute opened, when outside pressure reached 0.6 atmosphere, expected at roughly 26 kilometres altitude.

A rechargeable battery could power the instruments for 100 minutes, and the carrier's solar panels kept it charged during the journey. Finally, the whole station was sterilised to prevent biological contamination of Venus. The machine was ready. Would it leave on time?

articleEn: On 12 June 1967 a Molniya-M rocket lifted off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome with Venera 4 on top. Why the rush? The reason was the launch window: the few days of the year when the route from Earth to another planet needs the least energy. Venus and Earth come close to each other about every 1.6 years, and missing the chance would mean a very long wait.
That is why time was so tight. Remember the cracked electronics and cable brackets from the centrifuge test? They were replaced just before launch. The rocket rose and Venera 4 set off.

It was not a lone mission, though. The Soviet team had prepared two nearly identical 4V-1 probes. The second launched on 17 June and was named Kosmos 167, but it never got beyond low Earth orbit. One of the pair had already failed, and all hopes rested on Venera 4, travelling alone toward Venus.

Two days later, America sent its own Mariner 5, launched from Cape Canaveral on 14 June 1967 and also bound for Venus. Both spacecraft were heading for the same planet, and their data would later be examined together.

The long journey began. The carrier's solar panels kept the capsule's battery charged, while instruments such as the magnetometer measured space. But there was a big problem: even a tiny error in direction becomes enormous after millions of kilometres. On 29 July, with the probe 12,000,000 kilometres from Earth, the control team made a course correction. Without it, Venera 4 would have missed Venus.

Two corrections had been planned, and the station could receive and carry out 127 different commands from Earth. But the first correction was so accurate that the second was cancelled. After a poor start, this was good news.

Then came months of waiting. The probe travelled silently through space as 18 October slowly drew closer. The plan was for the carrier's instruments to work until entering Venus's atmosphere, then release the capsule and break apart. A small sphere was about to descend into an unknown world. Would it survive?

articleEn: On 18 October 1967 the carrier spacecraft finished its work and released the capsule. The Venera 4 lander began entering the atmosphere of Venus. Its expected landing site, a estimate at the time, was around 19 degrees North and 38 degrees East.

Then came the most dangerous phase. The capsule fell quickly and the heat shield reached 11,000 degrees Celsius. At one point the deceleration reached 300 G, three hundred times its own weight. Imagine what the instruments were going through. The capsule had been tested to 450 g, but now the test was not in a lab but in an alien sky. The capsule survived, and Venera 4 became the first spacecraft to survive entry into another planet's atmosphere.

At about 52 kilometres the parachute opened. The transmitters switched on and the capsule began sending pressure, temperature and gas composition data. The plan had expected this at about 26 kilometres. In reality the parachute opened at roughly twice that height. Venus was turning out to differ from the estimates.

Data came at just 1 bit per second, with a new measurement every 48 seconds, at 922 MHz. Several stations received it, including England's Jodrell Bank Observatory. Picture an extremely faint signal from deep space and large dishes on Earth straining to catch it. Each new bit opened a new world.

The first message was relatively mild. At 52 kilometres the temperature was 33 degrees Celsius and the pressure was less than 1 standard atmosphere. But as the capsule sank, every measurement showed temperature and pressure rising. The thick layers of atmosphere told a story very different from the old estimates. Inside the capsule the temperature was held at -8 degrees Celsius, and its temperature control kept working as the heat outside grew.

The whole descent lasted about 93 minutes. The part after the parachute opened covered about 26 kilometres, and new data kept arriving throughout. Then came the final measurement. By the end of those 26 kilometres the temperature had reached 262 degrees Celsius and the pressure 22 standard atmospheres: from 33 degrees to 262, and from less than 1 atmosphere to 22. The true face of Venus was emerging.

Then the signal stopped. The last bit arrived and silence fell. The team had only the numbers that had come in. The battery was built for 100 minutes and the descent lasted 93. One question remained: at what altitude was the capsule, really? For now it was enough that data had reached Earth from inside another planet for the first time. The question was what the numbers meant.

articleEn: Venera 4's instruments had measured the atmosphere of Venus from the inside for the first time. What is this air made of? The answer: 90 to 93 percent carbon dioxide, about 7 percent nitrogen, oxygen of only 0.4 to 0.8 percent, and water vapor of 0.1 to 1.6 percent. Venus's air is mostly the gas we breathe out, and with so little oxygen, breathing there is out of the question.

There was an interesting detail. The ratio of carbon dioxide to nitrogen was about 13. Some circles had expected the opposite ratio. The difference was so large that some scientists challenged the observations themselves. The first measurement of a new world, and already disputed! Sources differ slightly: one gives CO2 as 90 to 93 percent, another about 95 percent, while today's accepted value is 96.5 percent.

Next, the magnetic field. The carrier had a 2-metre magnetometer to measure it. The station found Venus's magnetic field very weak, about 3000 times weaker than Earth's, and no radiation belt. It was later understood that Venus's small magnetosphere is created by the solar wind, not by an internal dynamo.

Finding hydrogen and oxygen was the job of the carrier's ultraviolet spectrometer. The hydrogen corona turned out to be 1000 times less dense than Earth's, and no atomic oxygen was found. There was very little hydrogen in the outer atmosphere. All these results pointed one way: if Venus ever had water, it must have left the planet long ago.

This was unexpected, since Venus is covered by thick clouds. So little moisture beneath so many clouds? Today we know those clouds are actually sulfuric acid. Some studies suggest that liquid water may have existed on Venus billions of years ago.

For the first time, direct measurement showed that Venus is extremely hot and its air far denser than estimated. The capsule had been tested to 25 atmospheres. The measured pressure reached 22, and nobody knew what lay beyond. According to one source, Venera 4 showed that the surface temperature was higher than Mariner 2's estimate, close to 500 degrees Celsius. The data was so valuable that it helped shape the design of Venera 7, and engineers now knew better what kind of world lay ahead.
But a confusing question remained. What was the Soviet team's initial announcement? Did Venera 4 really reach the surface of Venus?

articleEn: So what was the Soviet team's first announcement, and why did it turn out wrong? The root of the story lies in one small instrument. Inside the capsule was a radar altimeter, whose job was to measure distance from the surface. It worked at 770 MHz. The principle was simple: the device sends a signal, catches the echo returning from below, and estimates altitude from that.

But the instrument had a weakness: a 30-kilometre ambiguity. The same signal could mean altitude X, or X plus 30, or X plus 60 kilometres. The trouble was that nobody then knew how high Venus's cloud tops were above the surface, so it was hard to judge.

When the altimeter gave its first return, the team read it as an altitude of 26 kilometres. Today it is thought the real altitude was about 55 kilometres. On the basis of this wrong reading, the Soviet team initially announced that the probe had reached the surface. That would have been huge news: the first spacecraft to reach another planet's surface intact.

But had it really happened? Doubts soon arose, and the result was quickly rejected. The first reason was that it did not match the planet's diameter as measured by radar. The second was the capsule's own pressure readings, which were far lower than the models newly made for Venus's environment. If it had reached the surface, the pressure should have been much higher. Two things were colliding, so one of them had to be wrong.

Meanwhile another spacecraft was nearing Venus: America's Mariner 5, and its timing was perfect. Mariner 5 flew past Venus on 19 October 1967, the day after Venera 4, at a distance of 3,990 kilometres. It carried a radio occultation experiment: when the spacecraft passes behind the planet, its radio signal travels through Venus's atmosphere.

When the two sets of data were analysed together, the surface pressure came out at 75 to 100 atmospheres. Remember that the hull of the Venera 4 capsule was strong for only 25 atmospheres. The surface pressure was three to four times that, so the capsule would have been crushed long before reaching the surface. Put simply, Venera 4 was never built to go that deep.
So the Soviet team withdrew its initial claim. That is not easy for a science team, but it is the real strength of science.

Still, one question remains. If the capsule did not reach the surface, where did the readings of 22 atmospheres and 262 degrees Celsius come from? The answer is that they were readings from the place where the signal ended, not the surface. The surface lay far below, in a much hotter and heavier environment.

articleEn: In 1969, under COSPAR, a joint Soviet–American working group studied the data from Venera 4 and Mariner 5 together. It was the Cold War, yet science sat two opposing camps at one table, an example of early space cooperation.

The result was clear. The surface of Venus is very hot and its environment far denser than estimated. By today's measurements, the average surface temperature is 464 degrees Celsius and the pressure 93 bar. Venera 4's last reading was 262 degrees Celsius and 22 atmospheres, so the surface pressure is more than four times that.

After this, Soviet engineers changed their strategy. They realised that the Venera 3 to 6 probes had not been built to withstand surface pressure. So Venera 5 and 6 were made atmospheric probes, shedding about half their payload before entering the atmosphere. Venera 5 sent data for 53 minutes and Venera 6 for 51 minutes. Both drifted slowly down on parachutes until their batteries ran out.

Then came Venera 7, launched in August 1970, the first probe designed to withstand surface conditions and make a soft landing. It was built stronger than necessary. On 15 December 1970 it reached the surface, although the parachute failed at the last moments and it tipped over. The signal was weak but kept coming for 23 minutes. It became the first human probe to send data from the surface of another planet.

Venera 7's switchboard was faulty and it got stuck in the temperature-sending position. Even so, scientists estimated the pressure from the temperature data. The result was 465 degrees Celsius and an estimated 90 atmospheres. These were the first direct measurements from the surface, and are very close to today's values.
And what of the sugar lock? Moisture on Venus turned out to be very low, so this water-triggered system was dropped from later probes.

The story that follows is even more astonishing. On 8 June 1975, Venera 9 sent the first pictures from the surface of another planet to Earth. In 1981, Venera 13 recorded sound. In 1983, Venera 15 and 16 used radar to map a large part of the northern hemisphere.

What is the lesson of this whole story? The first: keep checking your assumptions. One misread measurement can change the whole conclusion. The second: combining data from different sources is essential. Putting Venera 4 and Mariner 5 together made it possible to test the initial claim. And the third: failure teaches too. Venera 4 did not land on the surface, but it raised the questions that led to the next missions.

Yet Venus still keeps its secrets. According to some studies, liquid water may have existed there billions of years ago, before a runaway greenhouse effect changed everything. Another question is even more startling. About 50 kilometres above the surface, pressure and temperature are like those on Earth's surface. So could life be possible there? Some experts believe extremophile microorganisms might exist in the clouds. This is only speculation, and the 2020 phosphine claim was also disputed in later research.

Venera 4's descent into Venus's atmosphere lasted only 93 minutes, but it taught us that understanding new worlds takes patience, cooperation and the courage to tell the truth. shorts.roman: Ek chhota sa capsule 11,000 °C ki aag mein gir raha tha. Kya woh bach pata? Tareekh thi 18 October 1967, aur is capsule ka naam Venera 4 tha. Jab woh Venus ke atmosphere mein dakhil hua to is ki heat shield ka temperature 11,000 °C tak pahunch gaya. Ek lamhe par deceleration 300 G tak gayi, yani apne wazan se 300 guna zor. Phir taqriban 52 kilometre ki bulandi par parachute khula. Aur tareekh mein pehli bar kisi dusre sayyare ke andar se data zameen ki taraf aane laga. Venera 4 woh pehla spacecraft bana jo kisi dusre sayyare ke atmosphere mein dakhil ho kar bach nikla. Yeh safar 93 minutes jari raha. Lekin neeche kya intezar kar raha tha? Aakhri reading mein 262 °C aur 22 atmospheres thay, aur phir signal ruk gaya. Aakhir aage kya hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 18 October 1967, Venera 4 became the first spacecraft to survive entry into another planet's atmosphere.
Its heat shield hit 11,000 °C and it returned data during a 93-minute descent.

shorts.titleEn: Venus Air Measured for the First Time: Scientists Doubted It
shorts.text: Venus کی ہوا میں سانس لینا کیسا ہوتا؟ Venera 4 نے پہلی بار اس ہوا کو اندر سے ناپا۔ نتیجہ حیران کن تھا۔ 90 سے 93 فیصد carbon dioxide۔ تقریباً 7 فیصد nitrogen۔ Oxygen صرف 0.4 سے 0.8 فیصد، اور water vapor 0.1 سے 1.6 فیصد۔ یعنی وہاں سانس لینے کا سوال ہی نہیں تھا۔ دوستو، اصل جھٹکا کچھ اور تھا۔ Carbon dioxide اور nitrogen کا تناسب تقریباً 13 نکلا۔ کچھ حلقوں میں اس کا الٹ تناسب متوقع تھا۔ فرق اتنا بڑا تھا کہ کچھ scientists نے ان observations کو ہی challenge کر دیا۔ ایک نئی دنیا کی پہلی پیمائش، اور پہلی ہی پیمائش پر بحث! مزید یہ کہ نہ کوئی radiation belt ملا، نہ atomic oxygen۔ تو کیا آخرکار یہ نتیجے درست ثابت ہوئے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Venus ki hawa mein saans lena kaisa hota? Venera 4 ne pehli bar is hawa ko andar se napa. Nateeja hairan kun tha. 90 se 93 feesad carbon dioxide. Taqriban 7 feesad nitrogen. Oxygen sirf 0.4 se 0.8 feesad, aur water vapor 0.1 se 1.6 feesad. Yani wahan saans lene ka sawal hi nahi tha. Dostो, asal jhatka kuch aur tha. Carbon dioxide aur nitrogen ka tanasub taqriban 13 nikla. Kuch halqon mein is ka ulta tanasub mutawaqqa tha. Farq itna bara tha ke kuch scientists ne in observations ko hi challenge kar diya. Ek nayi duniya ki pehli paimaish, aur pehli hi paimaish par bahes! Mazeed yeh ke na koi radiation belt mila, na atomic oxygen. To kya aakhirkar yeh nateeje durust sabit hue? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Venera 4 measured the Venusian atmosphere from inside: 90–93% carbon dioxide and about 7% nitrogen.
The CO2-to-nitrogen ratio of about 13 was so surprising that some scientists contested it.

shorts.titleEn: The Radar Mistake That Fooled Soviet Scientists on Venus
shorts.text: ایک چھوٹی سی غلط فہمی نے Soviet scientists سے غلط اعلان کروا دیا۔ Venera 4 کے capsule میں 770 MHz کا radar altimeter لگا تھا۔ مسئلہ یہ تھا کہ اس میں 30 کلومیٹر کا ابہام تھا۔ یعنی ایک ہی signal X پر بھی آ سکتا تھا، X جمع 30 پر بھی، اور X جمع 60 پر بھی۔ اس وقت کسی کو معلوم نہیں تھا کہ Venus کے بادلوں کی اوپری تہہ سطح سے کتنی اونچی ہے۔ پہلا radar return دراصل تقریباً 55 کلومیٹر کی بلندی کا تھا، مگر اسے 26 کلومیٹر سمجھ لیا گیا۔ اسی بنیاد پر Soviet team نے ابتدا میں اعلان کیا کہ probe سطح تک پہنچ گیا۔ سوچیں، کتنا بڑا دعویٰ تھا! مگر یہ نتیجہ جلد ہی رد کر دیا گیا۔ آخر کیوں؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek chhoti si ghalat fehmi ne Soviet scientists se ghalat elaan karwa diya. Venera 4 ke capsule mein 770 MHz ka radar altimeter laga tha. Masla yeh tha ke is mein 30 kilometre ka ibham tha. Yani ek hi signal X par bhi aa sakta tha, X jama 30 par bhi, aur X jama 60 par bhi. Us waqt kisi ko maloom nahi tha ke Venus ke badlon ki upri tah satah se kitni unchi hai. Pehla radar return darasal taqriban 55 kilometre ki bulandi ka tha, magar ise 26 kilometre samajh liya gaya. Isi bunyad par Soviet team ne ibtida mein elaan kiya ke probe satah tak pahunch gaya. Sochein, kitna bara dawa tha! Magar yeh nateeja jald hi radd kar diya gaya. Aakhir kyun? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Venera 4's radar altimeter had a 30 km ambiguity, so a return from about 55 km was read as 26 km.
The Soviet team first announced the probe reached the surface, but the claim was soon dismissed.
